6.0.s.en: (1) The cry for help of a penitent

6.0.0.en: 1- Lord, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure.

6.0.1.en: 1- David acknowledges that he is a sinner and deserves punishment, but he approaches as a penitent and with the boldness of sonship, asking that God deal with him in His mercy; he deserves rebuke and discipline, but if only it might be in God's mercy and not in His anger and displeasure, because God's anger and displeasure destroy the sinful man, since the wages of sin is death (Rom 6:23).

6.0.2.en: 2- By this David's word does not contradict the saying of Paul the Apostle, "My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him" (Heb 12:5); indeed David himself said, "Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest" (Ps 94:12). David accepts discipline on earth but hopes that God will lift His anger from him on the day of judgment, for discipline by divine anger and displeasure is for the wicked on the day of judgment, whereas David, as a son, appeals to God's fatherhood to have compassion on him and rebuke him and discipline him with His love and mercy.

6.1.0.en: 2- Have mercy upon me, O Lord; for I am weak: O Lord, heal me; for my bones tremble.

6.1.1.en: 1- Here David confesses before God his weakness, and indeed the trembling of his bones, and bones are the strongest thing in a man's body, so he is no longer able to stand firm before God because of his sins, and this shows the extent of:

6.1.3.en: b- His sense of the fear of God.

6.1.4.en: 2- David felt weakness in the following:

6.1.5.en: a- Spiritual weakness because of his fall into sin, which may be his fall with the wife of Uriah the Hittite.

6.1.6.en: b- Psychological weakness resulting from the fall into sin, "My soul is also sore vexed" (v. 3).

6.1.7.en: c- Bodily weakness represented by the trembling of the bones.

6.1.8.en: d- His fear of his enemies and those who trouble him (v. 7). Because of this weakness David asks God's mercy and healing with his whole being.

6.2.0.en: 3- My soul is also sore vexed: but thou, O Lord, how long?

6.2.1.en: 1- David asked for God's mercy and that He not discipline him in anger and displeasure in (v. 1) because of what he mentioned in (vv. 2, 3), namely his weakness and trembling and shaking. By this he represents the perfect penitent.

6.2.2.en: 2- At the same time he urges God to answer quickly and not leave him in this hard state. But why does God delay in these situations and leave the penitent to suffer?

6.2.3.en: a- That their repentance may be completed with contrition, humility, tears and patience.

6.2.4.en: b- That they may be sure of the gravity of sin, and so keep away from everything that leads to it.

6.2.5.en: c- That their faith and hope in God and their spiritual fervor may increase.

6.2.6.en: d- That they may long for the life of righteousness, purity and spiritual loftiness.

6.3.0.en: 4- Return, O Lord, deliver my soul: oh save me for thy mercies' sake.

6.3.1.en: 1- At the end of his cry for help David expresses his intense longings for the return of God's tenderness and mercy upon him, that He not leave him in the torment of the consequences of his sin, but return to His former fatherly kindnesses toward him and rescue him from the sin into which he had cast himself, so that He mends his faults by divine mercy and saves him, that he may return to enjoy God's embrace and pray with joy and praise God.

6.3.2.en: 2- David feels that sin makes him a stranger to God, so he asks God to bring him back to Himself after he had strayed, so he enjoys God's return to him in mercy, and is rescued and saved from all evil.

6.3.3.en: 3- In God's return, which David asks for, there is the following meaning:

6.3.4.en: a- The return of His mercy to rescue him and save him instead of His anger and displeasure.

6.3.5.en: b- The bringing back of David, who had gone far away through sin, to return to God.

6.3.6.en: c- The return of God's appearing in David's life, that is, David enjoys, as a son, the sight of God.

6.3.7.en: In proportion to your repentance, humility and lowliness before God, His mercies overflow upon you. And do not be troubled if His answer is delayed, for His fatherhood wants you to complete your repentance in order to receive great salvation and joy.

6.4.0.en: 5- For in death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?

6.4.1.en: 1- David feels that sin separates him from God, so he is like one dead with regard to God, and like one who has fallen into the abyss of evil, so he cannot pray and praise God because of his immersion in sin.

6.4.2.en: 2- Sin leads to eternal death if man does not repent of it, and consequently there in the abyss and hell no one can remember God and praise Him, because he receives his eternal punishment.

6.4.3.en: 3- On the contrary, the bodily death of the righteous does not hinder them from continuing praise and prayer, but they set out in them with greater power, as we say in the Third Hoos and call the spirits and souls of the righteous who are in heaven to share praise with us (Dan 3:86, that is, the Additions to Daniel).

6.4.4.en: 4- The meaning of this is that our life on earth is an opportunity for prayer and praise, but after death our opportunity for repentance, prayer and returning to God has ended, and what remains is facing eternal punishment.

6.5.0.en: 6- I am weary with my groaning; every night I make my bed to swim; I melt my couch with my tears.

6.5.1.en: 1- This verse shows the depth of David's repentance, which appears in his continual heartache over his sin, so that in the end he became tired psychologically and physically. It is clear that the repentance continued a long time, so that he said "I am weary"; in addition, he is still in the present making his bed swim and melting in his couch, that is, he continues in repentance. Repentance is not a moment but a life; however confident the penitent is of God's forgiveness, as a son he is deeply moved by what he did against his father through the sins he committed.

6.5.2.en: 2- From the foregoing the importance is understood of man's examining himself every day, whether concerning a sin he committed recently or some time ago, so he finds his heart sighing and deeply moved, and so he lives the life of repentance.

6.5.3.en: 3- His feelings did not stop at the limit of sighing, but his tears flowed abundantly, so that he said "every night I make my bed to swim", that is, he wept for many hours.

6.5.4.en: 4- During the day King David was occupied with his responsibilities in running the kingdom, but his authority and works did not distract his heart from being alone at night to examine himself and stand before the just Judge, and so he wept much. For whoever can stand before God on the day of judgment, whatever his position, is nothing. Thus David was contrite with many tears, so he lived repentance in its depths and received countless blessings, and God led his life all his days. Although David defiled his bed once, he makes his bed swim every night. Although David committed his sin in the night and the darkness, he turns his night by the tears of repentance into a bright life with God, so he received God's countless mercies.

6.5.5.en: 5- Repentance is considered a second Baptism; as man is immersed in the water of Baptism, so also man is immersed in a sea of tears that he pours out before God, when he examines himself and repents of his sins, so his life is renewed every day through the sacrament of repentance and confession. David did not say "I wet my bed" but said "I make to swim", and this means that his tears were very abundant, and his repentance consequently was deep.

6.5.6.en: 6- David shows the multitude of his tears in that his bed was melting from the abundant tears, so he was not absorbed in his sleep but occupied with repentance every night, and on the contrary the lax soul, we express it in the interruption of sleep by the prayer of the Agpeya, that it is "cast down upon the bed of sins and negligent in subduing the body"; that is, David was on his bed as though in a sea, because the bed had melted from the multitude of tears, so David was swimming in these tears.

6.6.0.en: 7- Mine eye is consumed because of grief; it waxeth old because of all mine enemies.

6.6.1.en: Consumed: sank in and was troubled.

6.6.2.en: 1- David was angry with himself because of his fall into sin, so his tears flowed from his eyes until his eyes sank in with tears and were covered in deep repentance.

6.6.3.en: 2- His eyes also sank in from his remembering God's anger against him because of his sin, so his tears flowed, seeking by repentance His forgiveness and mercies.

6.6.4.en: 3- From the multitude of tears David's eyes were consumed, that is, his eyes became like the eyes of an old man, weak and wasted, as he remembered his spiritual enemies, that is, the demons who made him fall into sin, and he offered regret in many tears.

6.6.5.en: 4- But the wonder is that David enjoyed peace of heart during this repentance and abundant tears, so he was able to continue in repentance all the days of his life, for he was confident of the word of Nathan the prophet that the Lord had put away his sin, but this did not keep him from seeing God, the fearful Judge, so there was mixed in his life intense regret, appearing in many tears, with the deep peace that God bestowed on him all his life. It is a peace that cannot be experienced outside repentance.

6.6.6.en: If, my brother, you need true peace, come with me, let us repent of our sins, and stand before the fearful God and let our eyes express what is within us, remembering the guilt of our sins, and so receive His forgiveness and His many divine blessings.

6.7.0.en: 8- Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity; for the Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping.

6.7.1.en: 1- When God gave peace in David's heart he became reassured and his faith was firm, so he called all his enemies the demons and all the wicked who followed them, who gloated over him and fight him, to depart from him. The power on which he relies is God, who heard his prayers, and even accepted his tears and his contrition before Him, and consequently God is with him, defending him and protecting him, after He accepted him and forgave his sins.

6.7.2.en: 2- Here we see that weeping is a feeling of deep repentance that has a voice stronger than the ordinary cries of human beings, because weeping springs from heartfelt feelings, regretful and humbled before God.

6.7.3.en: 3- And we see clearly the power of faith of one who repents and is contrite before God, for he speaks with confidence that God has heard the voice of his weeping, and this means that God gave him this confidence in his heart, until he uttered these words.

6.8.0.en: 9- The Lord hath heard my supplication; the Lord will receive my prayer.

6.8.1.en: 1- Supplications are prayers filled with humility and faith, for in them we lay hold of God, who cannot fail the one who clings to Him; therefore David said the Lord has heard, that is, in the past tense, for he is reassured that his supplications have reached God.

6.8.2.en: 2- The humble receives God's mercies and tenderness, and God accepts his prayers and lifts him out of his tribulations, however great his weakness.

6.9.0.en: 10- Let all mine enemies be ashamed and sore vexed: let them return and be ashamed suddenly.

6.9.1.en: 1- David continues his speech in the faith of the penitent whose prayer God has answered, and he affirms that all the wicked and the demons will be ashamed and greatly afraid when they see God's power supporting him, since he has been changed from a rejected sinner into an accepted son, and his heavenly Father even protects him, all this through repentance.

6.9.2.en: 2- Indeed all his labor in repentance and spiritual striving throughout his life becomes nothing before God's acceptance of him on the day of judgment, when He glorifies him with His saints, so all the long time he has passed through is not counted, for he says "suddenly", when he looks upon the glories of heaven.

6.9.3.en: 3- On the other hand he makes clear that the demons around him, who rejoiced at his fall, depart and are ashamed and tremble when God suddenly appears and declares His acceptance of his repentance, for repentance transfers man from under the authority of the devil to the dignity and glory of God's children.

6.9.4.en: 4- Perhaps David in this verse, when he shows the wicked their shame before God's power, is thereby calling them to stop their evils and repent.

6.9.5.en: Be confident that God hears your prayers and supplications and tears and that He is very near to you, to blot out your sins and strengthen you and raise you above the demons who made you fall.

6.9.6.en: God saves the innocent and punishes the wicked A Shiggaion of David, which he sang unto the Lord, concerning the words of Cush the Benjamite. "O Lord my God, in thee do I put my trust" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

6.9.7.en: 1- Its writer: the prophet David, who had been exposed to evil speech and false accusations, so he said this Psalm, beseeching God to look upon his innocence and save him from the one who accuses him falsely.

6.9.8.en: 2- Cush the Benjamite is a person whose name is not mentioned except in this place, and he is a known figure from the tribe of Benjamin, from which King Saul came, who pursued David and tried many times to kill him. It is understood from this that Cush was hostile to David, a follower, like most of his tribe, of Saul, and he said many words that were false accusations against David.

6.9.9.en: 3- This Psalm shows David's supplication to God, who is able to rescue him from his enemies and show his innocence, because He blesses and rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked, and David believes in God and trusts in Him with all his heart.

6.9.10.en: 4- We see in the title of this Psalm that it is a Shiggaion, from the word shajw, that is, sorrow, so it is a sorrowful lament that David offers to God from his soul affected by the wrongs of his enemies, and he takes refuge in God who is able to console him.

6.9.11.en: 5- This Psalm is considered one of the Messianic Psalms, which prophesy about Christ the awaited Messiah, as it prophesied about the resurrection of Christ and His ascension, because David is a type of Christ, and it is also considered one of the royal Psalms, because it speaks about King David.

7.0.0.en: 1- O Lord my God, in thee do I put my trust: save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me.

7.0.1.en: 1- We sense in David's words here his strong relationship with God, for he says O Lord, and by it he means Jehovah, the God of the whole world, and then he says my God, who is personally bound to him, and with whom he has boldness, and this encouraged him to ask in faith, despite the difficulty of the trials he is passing through.

7.0.2.en: 2- Since David believed in God he relied on Him, and this gave him reassurance, despite the rising up of the wicked against him, so he prayed this prayer, seeking the help of God, who will certainly save him.

7.0.3.en: 3- He asked for salvation and deliverance from those who pursue him, and perhaps by this he means Saul and his pursuits of him, or Absalom his son, who drove him out and removed him from his throne, and his emphasis on asking for salvation and deliverance shows:

7.0.4.en: a- The extent of the distress he is passing through.

7.0.5.en: b- His faith and his clinging to God.

7.0.6.en: 4- We note David's love for his enemies in that he asked God to save him and deliver him from the hands of his pursuers but did not ask for vengeance on them.

7.1.0.en: 2- Lest he tear my soul like a lion, rending it in pieces, while there is none to deliver.

7.1.2.en: 1- If David spoke in the previous verse about his pursuers in the plural, in this verse he speaks about them in the singular, that is, the lion; because he is confident that Satan is his only enemy who moves the wicked against him. This helps David to love his enemies, and to be spiritually alert and rely on God, because his war is with Satan.

7.1.3.en: 2- He used the comparison with the lion, since it is the king of the forest and the strongest of the animals, and he understands this well as a shepherd of sheep, guarding against the lion that snatches his lambs. On the other hand Saul, who pursued him, was a king, so he is like the lion. And Absalom also seized the kingdom from David, that is, both of them were kings.

7.1.4.en: 3- And Peter the Apostle likens Satan to the lion, but David is confident that Christ, the true Lion who came out of the tribe of Judah, is the One able to save him from Satan.

7.1.5.en: It is good to know that your true enemy is Satan alone, so that you prepare with all your spiritual weapons of prayers, fasts and humility, and so defeat Satan easily, especially when you love the one who wrongs you and pray for him.

7.2.0.en: 3- O Lord my God, if I have done this; if there be iniquity in my hands; 4- If I have rewarded evil unto him that was at peace with me, and have plundered him that troubled me without cause.

7.2.1.en: 1- David in his distress casts himself before God, declaring his innocence regarding his enemies, for he did not wrong them or do evil to them, and yet they rose up against him, pursuing him and trying to kill him. Consequently he beseeches God to save him, for the sake of his weakness and innocence. He satisfies divine justice by his innocence and asks mercy from the tender God, for the sake of his weakness.

7.2.2.en: 2- David says "if I have done this" (v. 3), and he means pursuing and trying to kill any innocent person who did not wrong him, as Saul does to him, or if I have risen up against my father to kill him and seize his glory, as Absalom my son did to me.

7.2.3.en: 3- David passed through the degrees of love in dealing with others, which are:

7.2.4.en: a- Meeting good with evil: "if I have rewarded evil unto him that was at peace with me" (v. 4), and this is the degree of barbarism, that is, before the Mosaic Law, and even against the good human conscience.

7.2.5.en: b- Meeting evil with evil: "have plundered him that troubled me without cause" (v. 4), that is, he did not wrong the one who troubled him and wronged him. And this is the law of the Old Testament, that is, "eye for eye, tooth for tooth"

7.2.7.en: c- Meeting evil with good; this is what David did, for he asked for salvation and deliverance from the hands of his pursuers and did not ask for vengeance, but pardoned them, as he said to Saul after he fell into his hands (1 Sam 24:11), and as he asked Joab the commander of his army to deal gently with his son Absalom, who was trying to kill him (2 Sam 18:5). And this is the law of Christianity, that is, love of enemies (Mt 5:44).

7.3.0.en: 5- Let the enemy persecute my soul, and take it; yea, let him tread down my life upon the earth, and lay mine honour in the dust. Selah.

7.3.1.en: 1- David declares his deserving of humiliation and punishment if he has done the injustice and evils mentioned previously in (vv. 3, 4), for he is subject to divine justice and accepts God's discipline. But if he has not done evil, he asks God's mercies. David shows that if he had done these previous evils, he deserves what Saul or Absalom is doing to him, but if he has not done them, he is confident that the just God will save him.

7.3.2.en: 2- Virtue is the new life with God, that is, David's love for his enemies and his doing good and not wronging without cause, so if David had done the opposite of these virtues, he deserves that his life be trodden down to the earth, that is, be humiliated and die. He also deserves to lose his glory as king.

7.3.3.en: 3- By glory he also means his glorious eternal life, for he does not deserve it if he has not lived in virtue, and his glory is laid in the dust, that is, he goes down to hell.

7.3.4.en: 4- And whoever does not practice virtues, his life is trodden down to the earth, that is, he becomes earthly and carnal, behaving like the rest of the wicked human beings, and has no glory before God.

7.3.5.en: 5- The word Selah is a musical pause to reflect on the punishment of sin, to keep away from it and from all its sources.

7.3.6.en: Take care to examine yourself every day, to discover your sins, so you are purified and consequently deserve the divine mercies.

7.4.0.en: 6- Arise, O Lord, in thine anger, lift up thyself because of the rage of mine enemies: and attend to me; in truth thou hast commanded.

7.4.1.en: 1- When David felt the strength of the enemies who pursue him and their authority, his heart was not shaken because of his faith in the mighty God, whose power is above every power in the world. So he called upon the Lord in this prayer to arise in His anger, that is, to come out of His long-suffering to discipline the wicked, and declare His rejection of him, and thereby rescue David his son.

7.4.2.en: 2- He also calls upon the Lord to lift Himself above the height of the anger of those who oppose him; if their anger is severe and has become rage, God's anger is stronger and rises above their anger to discipline them and show them their weakness, so that they do not persist in their evils.

7.4.3.en: 3- The rising of God's anger against the opponents is not only to stop their anger and their opposition to David, but God is also able to draw them to Himself and turn them into believers in Him, submissive to Him, and consequently at peace with David, as God turned Abimelech king of Gerar to be at peace with Isaac and to make a covenant with him (Gen 26:26-30). And likewise Laban, submissive and at peace with Jacob and making a covenant with him also, so that Jacob would not harm him, because God was with him (Gen 31:48-52).

7.4.4.en: 4- By David's prayer the battle was turned from a war between him and his opponents into a war between God and the wicked, and by this David was reassured, because no one can stand before God.

7.4.5.en: 5- This verse speaks about Christ: "Arise" signifies the resurrection of Christ, which shattered the forces of evil, and "lift up thyself" signifies His being lifted up on the Cross to bind Satan, so the rising of God's anger above the anger of Satan, who opposes mankind, was accomplished on the Cross.

7.4.6.en: 6- He calls upon God to attend to him, and this does not mean that God was heedless or forgetful, but he intends to move God's mercies, so that He rescues him from his enemies.

7.4.7.en: 7- David relies on God's justice, so he says to Him: "in truth thou hast commanded", and here is David the innocent, wronged by his opponents, so he deserves God's mercies and help.

7.5.0.en: 7- And the assembly of the tribes shall compass thee about: therefore return thou over it on high.

7.5.1.en: 1- David speaks by the spirit of prophecy about the gathering of the peoples around God and His king David, and God's returning to reign over their hearts, and this is what happened after David reigned, and the kingdom in his days extended from the Euphrates to the river of Egypt, and the peoples submitted to him and to his God.

7.5.2.en: 2- It is a clear prophecy about the faith of the tribes of the world in Christ, and not only the Jews, and His returning to reign over the hearts of those who believe in Him in the whole world.

7.5.3.en: 3- It is likewise a clear prophecy about the ascension of Christ into heaven and His return to His glory, after He had completed redemption on the Cross and the resurrection from the dead.

7.5.4.en: 4- Perhaps this verse signifies what will happen on the day of judgment, when Christ the Judge appears on high with all the nations of the world around Him, and He judges them, and then gathers His children who believe in Him, that they may surround Him in the Kingdom of Heaven and He glorifies them with Him.

7.5.5.en: Have a direct relationship with God in prayer, and cast all your problems upon Him, and be no more troubled by those who oppose you, because God is the one who protects you and defends you, and pray for those who oppose you, that they may return to God.

7.6.0.en: 8- The Lord shall judge the people: judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, and according to mine integrity that is in me.

7.6.1.en: 1- David the wronged hopes for God's justice to save him from his opponents, and he declares that God will judge all the peoples of the earth on the day of judgment. He does not fear the day of judgment, because he has reached a high degree of love for God, as the Holy Bible says, "perfect love casteth out fear" (1 Jn 4:18).

7.6.2.en: 2- David as one wronged awaits his right which the unjust took from him, that God may compensate him for it, as a free grace, because there is no power in himself, but it is God's grace.

7.6.3.en: 3- When David says "according to mine integrity" he means the relative perfection that he reached as a weak human being, that is, according to my obedience to Your commandments deliver me and reward me, that my heart may be comforted.

7.6.4.en: 4- David hopes not only for earthly salvation from his enemies and opponents but for the eternal reward, where the heavenly glories are.

7.7.0.en: 9- Oh let the wickedness of the wicked come to an end; but establish the just: for the righteous God trieth the hearts and reins.

7.7.1.en: 1- David asks God the Judge to judge evil and bring it to an end, and this is accomplished on the day of judgment, when God binds Satan and casts him into eternal torment, he and all the wicked who submitted to him.

7.7.2.en: 2- David also desires that the wickedness of the wicked come to an end, and not the life of the wicked, that is, that God remove evil from them and they repent.

7.7.3.en: 3- The purpose of David's request for the end of evil is that the just may not be shaken or exposed to going astray, and therefore David asks God to establish the just, and he means himself and every person who believes in God and lives with Him.

7.7.4.en: 4- God the Judge does not need proofs like the rest of the judges, because He trieth the hearts and reins, that is, He knows the thoughts and intentions of every person, and He is the righteous and holy One, who easily uncovers any evil inside human beings and is repelled by it, so God judges evil.

7.7.5.en: 5- The complete end of evil is the day of judgment, as we mentioned, and the complete establishment of the just is in the Kingdom of Heaven.

7.8.0.en: 10- My shield is with God, who saveth the upright in heart.

7.8.1.en: 1- In faith David declares that his protection is in God, and he likens this protection to the shield with which the soldier wards off the enemy's arrows from himself, for God is the One who protects His children from the arrows of the devil and his wars.

7.8.2.en: 2- David is also confident that God is the Savior, but of those who believe in Him, and are upright, not only in their outward conduct but also in their hearts, that is, their thoughts and inner intentions.

7.8.3.en: Ask God's protection, confident that He loves you, and let your heart be upright before Him through repentance, so you are pure by His forgiveness and enjoy His love.

7.9.0.en: 11- God is a righteous judge, and a God who is angry every day.

7.9.1.en: 1- David reminds himself and all mankind that God will judge the whole world, and He is just, He will show partiality to no one, and He knows all the evils of human beings.

7.9.2.en: 2- Because of the evils of human beings God is very angry every day, for human beings do not cease from wrongdoing, but He is long-suffering and does not punish them, giving them an opportunity for repentance. But if they are negligent He will be compelled to punish them, because He cannot abandon His justice.

7.9.3.en: 3- Indignation declares the strength and sternness of God's anger; He is not silent because He is weak, but because He is merciful and long-suffering and wants everyone to return to Him through repentance.

7.10.0.en: 12- If he turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready,

7.10.1.en: 1- In His long-suffering God awaits the repentance of the wicked, and if they do not return to Him by repentance He draws His sword and whets it, that is, makes it sharpened and keen, ready to cut. This signifies God's warnings of punishment for the wicked. God is long-suffering; when He sees the wicked persisting in their evil He does not hasten their punishment, despite their disregard of His long-suffering, but also warns them with the words of the Holy Bible, that they may repent.

7.10.2.en: 2- And to confirm God's warnings the prophet says that God bends His bow and makes it ready, to strike the wicked with His arrows.

7.10.3.en: 3- God's word is the sword, which cuts off evil and strikes hearts like arrows, that they may be moved and return to Him by repentance. But if they insist on not returning, the sword or the arrows kill them. God was long-suffering toward King Saul, but he persisted in evil, so He warned him through the mouth of Samuel, and by his seeing David the righteous as an example of goodness, but Saul made light of all this, so he was killed in the war when he was struck by an arrow, and then fell upon the sword and died (1 Sam 31:3, 4).

7.10.4.en: 4- The sword kills those who are near, while the arrows kill those who are far, so God warns the wrongdoers whose sins are visible and near and clear, and likewise those who hid their sins in their hearts, or were negligent and exposed to falling into sins that are still far from them, but will come to them and fight them.

7.11.0.en: 13- He hath also aimed at him the instrument of death; he maketh his arrows burning.

7.11.1.en: God continues in His long-suffering, so He aims, that is, directs His fiery arrows, to kill and burn, that is, they must destroy and kill the wicked, but He has not yet sent them, but threatens to send them, that is, warns the wicked that they may repent, so His tenderness is wonderful beyond description, even toward those who oppose Him and disobey Him.

7.12.0.en: 14- Behold, he travaileth with iniquity, and hath conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood.

7.12.1.en: 1- In this verse he speaks about the stages of sin, which are conception, then travail, then birth, that is, evil increases and is perfected gradually, although the woman gives birth to a child, that is, a new life in the world, but the wicked gives birth to iniquity.

7.12.2.en: 2- He put the stage of travail before conception, because the wicked person feels the pains of lust and evil within him from the beginning of sin.

7.12.3.en: 3- On the other side, the just conceives and gives birth to the fruits of the Holy Spirit, and although he suffers the pains of travail, they are the labors of spiritual striving and with them are God's consolations, and in the end he receives great blessings.

7.13.0.en: 15- He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made. 16- His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate.

7.13.2.en: A pit: a hole in the ground that fills with water from the rain, so it becomes like a pool.

7.13.3.en: The wicked digs a pit to make his brother fall, and he falls into it himself, that is, his evil returns upon his head. And this happened to many, such as Haman, who tried to kill Mordecai by hanging him on a gallows, and the king killed him and hanged him on the same gallows (Esth 7:9, 10); and likewise the two elders tried to kill Susanna, and the people killed them (Dan 14:28, 41); and also Absalom tried to kill David his father, and he was killed in the war (2 Sam 1:6-10); and Saul also tried to kill David and was killed in the war (2 Sam 18:9).

7.13.4.en: Do not think evil of others, whether by evil suspicion or by condemnation, lest God condemn you and the evil in you harm you, but make excuses for everyone, however they have erred, and pray for them.

7.14.0.en: 17- I will praise the Lord according to his righteousness: and will sing praise to the name of the Lord most high.

7.14.1.en: 1- David ends the Psalm with praise of God and thanksgiving to Him, because He delivers His righteous children and punishes the wicked.

7.14.2.en: 2- It is beautiful that David begins the Psalm with reliance on God and ends it with praise, for this is the life of those who rely on God, that they rejoice in the end and give thanks to God, whatever the tribulations they passed through.

7.14.3.en: Let thanksgiving be an essential part of your prayer every day, that your heart may rejoice, and you may rejoice the heart of God, and His blessings upon you may increase.

7.14.4.en: The glory of God in man To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm of David. "O Lord our Lord, how excellent is thy name" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

7.14.5.en: 1- Its writer: the prophet David, as appears from the title.

7.14.6.en: 2- It is a Psalm of praise and glorification of God.

7.14.7.en: 3- This Psalm is sung before a large assembly, for we find in its title that it is for the chief Musician, that is, a group of singers sing it under the leadership of a conductor, or leader.

7.14.8.en: 4- The repetition of this Psalm is accompanied by a musical instrument called the Gittith because it is taken from the city of Gath. By the Gittith may be meant a tune taken from the city of Gath, and it is the tune of this Psalm. By the Gittith may also be meant a winepress, because Gath is a Hebrew word meaning a winepress, and in the Septuagint the title of this Psalm is written "for the winepresses", and this points to Christ, who passed through the winepress alone and died for us, as appears in (v. 5), where it says "thou hast made him a little lower than the angels", that is, Christ in His death on the Cross was without honor because of His love for us.

7.14.9.en: 5- This Psalm shows the position of man in the heart of God and God's honoring him, for he is the head of all creation.

7.14.10.en: 6- This Psalm is considered one of the Messianic Psalms, because it speaks about the glorified Christ, who condescended by His Incarnation to redeem us.

7.14.11.en: 7- The New Testament gives attention to this Psalm, for it quoted from it three times; Christ Himself mentioned it in (Mt 21:16) and Paul the Apostle quoted from it in (1 Cor 15:27), (Heb 2:6-8).

7.14.12.en: 8- In the original Hebrew this Psalm has eight verses, and the name Jehovah is mentioned in the first and the eighth verse, and this points to the fact that Jehovah is the First and the Last, because the number 8 signifies eternity. (1) The greatness of G (vv. 1-3)
